topicName: Structured Streaming Architecture and Time Handling
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Structured Streaming Architecture and Time Handling in Apache Spark"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Apache Spark Structured Streaming is a scalable and fault-tolerant stream processing engine built on the Spark SQL engine. It allows you to express streaming computations the same way you would express batch computations on static data, leveraging the Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Architecture of Structured Streaming"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"At the heart of Structured Streaming is the concept of the Unbounded Table. As streaming data arrives from sources like Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, or file systems, it is continuously appended to an input unbounded table. Every time new data arrives, a query processes it through a trigger interval, producing results that go into the result table."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Input Source: Receives raw data and converts it into a DataFrame or Dataset."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Query Execution: Spark continuously checks for new data, applies transformations, and updates the result table based on the configured output mode."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Output Sink: Writes the updated results to external systems such as Delta Lake, databases, or message brokers."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Time Handling in Streaming"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Handling time correctly is critical for stateful operations like windowed aggregations. Spark distinguishes between two types of time: Processing Time and Event Time."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Processing Time: The time on the machine processing the data. It is easy to use but prone to out-of-order data issues."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Event Time: The time embedded in the data itself (e.g., when a user clicks a button). It is robust against network delays and system failures."},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"Implementing Event Time and Watermarking"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Because networks can delay messages, event-driven streams often receive late data. Spark uses Watermarking to allow the engine to automatically track event time and clean up old state. A watermark tells the engine how long to wait for late data."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import window, col

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName("StructuredStreamingTimeHandling") \
    .getOrCreate()

# Read streaming data from a socket source
lines = spark.readStream \
    .format("socket") \
    .option("host", "localhost") \
    .option("port", 9999) \
    .load()

# Assuming data format: timestamp, word
words = lines.select(
    col("value").cast("timestamp").alias("timestamp"),
    col("value").alias("word")
)

# Apply watermark and tumbling window aggregation
windowedCounts = words \
    .withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes") \
    .groupBy(
        window(col("timestamp"), "5 minutes"),
        col("word")
    ).count()

# Write output to console
query = windowedCounts.writeStream \
    .outputMode("update") \
    .format("console") \
    .option("truncate", "false") \
    .start()

query.awaitTermination()"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"By combining Structured Streaming architecture with robust event time management and watermarking, Apache Spark enables developers to build complex, low-latency, and stateful real-time data pipelines that accurately handle out-of-order data."}]
